extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, manuscript referees, and researchers studying peer review (psychology and related sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedural recommendations for evaluating manuscripts and for conducting/improving journal peer-review (referee behavior, editorial responsibilities, reviewer training, and use of rating forms). Focused on psychological/behavioral science journals but applicable broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable reader interest in the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Probable reader interest in the problem (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 1 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. 4-point scale. Source: Based on Scott 1974.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of present contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of present contribution (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 2 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. 4-point scale. Empirically rated by reviewers as the most relevant criterion for final recommendation (correlations R = .71 and .73).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to relevant literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to relevant literature (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 3 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. 4-point scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of research
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of research (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 4 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. Scored on a 10-point scale relative to average JAP article. To be disregarded for case reports and theoretical articles (note c). Empirically the second-most relevant attribute for publication decisions (correlations R = .63 and .62).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of data (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 5 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. Scored on a 10-point scale relative to average JAP article. To be disregarded for case reports and theoretical articles (note c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and organization of the material presented
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and organization of the material presented (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 6 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. 4-point scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Succinctness (Table 1, Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item 7 on the JAP manuscript attribute rater form. 4-point scale. Empirically regarded as the least relevant checklist criterion for publication decisions (correlations R = .32 and .37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weighting of manuscript attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers tend to agree on the relative importance of manuscript attributes: 'importance' is most relevant, 'research design' next, 'succinctness' least, with other checklist criteria intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical correlations reported (e.g., importance R = .71/.73; design R = .63/.62; succinctness R = .32/.37; other items range .38–.46). However, agreement on weights does not imply agreement on which manuscripts receive which scores (i.e., agreement about weights but not about manuscript ratings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rating forms and reviewer training (caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of more sophisticated manuscript attribute rating forms and training reviewers to map checklist scores to publishability is proposed but evidence suggests limited benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicchetti & Eron found lower interreviewer agreement when a 7-item rating form was used (R_intraclass = .15) versus manuscripts evaluated without the form (R = .21). Other journals achieved high agreement without rating forms. Recommendation: be cautious; training and forms may not improve review quality and can be futile unless validated empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize accuracy of individual reviewers over inter-reviewer agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and improvement efforts should focus on the accuracy of individual reviewers rather than solely on agreement between reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone argues that developing accuracy criteria would allow determination of which reviewers perform more creditably (e.g., whether apparent bias or superior discrimination explains divergent outcomes). Research should define objective accuracy standards against which reviewer judgments can be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train reviewers to detect crucial methodological flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to detect fatal or crucial flaws in research design is a key reviewer skill and can be objectified and taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone suggests 'crucial-flaw-discovering' is a teachable skill requiring more refined technology and training; reviewer training programs should include instruction in detecting design/analysis flaws that invalidate conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural editorial remedy: author rebuttal + independent arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: When editors lack sufficient expertise to evaluate unfavorable referee reports, authors should receive referees' criticisms and be invited to rebut; the manuscript plus criticisms and rebuttals should be sent to an independent arbiter for final verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by A. M. Colman as a procedure used successfully by some journals (Current Psychological Research; Current Psychological Reviews) to correct referee error and obvious injustices in the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify explicit criteria for acceptable papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and research into peer review should work to specify a set of ingredients/criteria that acceptable papers should include, which could be agreed upon by competent reviewers/editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone recommends research address specifying criteria for acceptable papers; while absolute standards may not exist, a practical, explicit set of attributes could improve consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop procedures for monitoring and maintaining reviewer accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement systems to monitor the continued accuracy of trained reviewers and maintain reviewer performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone calls for procedures to monitor reviewers' accuracy over time; suggestions include performance-dependent selection/retention on editorial boards or other incentives to maintain accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish reward systems to sustain high-quality reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Create incentives or rewards (financial or career-based) to encourage consistent, high-level reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone notes reviews are under-recognized and suggests rewarding reviewers—options include payment or performance-dependent editorial appointments—to sustain reviewer commitment and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screen reviewers for competence before assigning reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should screen potential reviewers to ensure they are competent to evaluate particular manuscripts before sending out reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crandall recommends proactive screening to avoid incompetent or overextended reviewers; selecting appropriate experts can reduce erroneous or irrelevant reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screen returned reviews to eliminate gratuitous or irrelevant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Returned reviews should be checked by editors to remove gratuitous insults, irrelevant criticisms, or nonconcrete generalities before acting on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crandall suggests screening reviews as they are returned to eliminate unhelpful comments; editors should act to protect authors from gratuitous or abusive remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one thorough expert editorial read with balanced judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond referee reports, at least one knowledgeable, mature, expert should read the manuscript and all reviews and provide a balanced editorial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crandall argues that a single thorough expert read can provide the 'mature, balanced, editorial wisdom' ideal for decision-making and help correct misguided referee recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of blind (anonymized) review to reduce status bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind (author-anonymized) review should be used to minimize bias based on author/institution status unless evidence supports unblinded review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crandall changes stance in light of Peters & Ceci results: blind review recommended as a safeguard against bias from author/institution prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage objective, evidence-based reviews; consider signed reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should provide objective evidence and documentation in their criticisms; signed reviews are advocated to encourage factual, impartial, documented evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DeBakey recommends signed reviews to discourage vague, unanchored generalities and to require reviewers to provide supporting evidence for criticisms, which may reduce gratuitous or biased judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting author-identity clues and guarding against recognition biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers/editors should be aware that anonymity can be compromised by clues (e.g., self-citations, distinctive content, fictitious institutions) and take steps to reduce recognition biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DeBakey raises concerns that references, institutional names, and other clues can reveal author identity; editors should be mindful of these cues when seeking anonymous review and consider their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agenda and institutional support for peer-review studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Call for more empirical research on the peer-review process and for professional societies to support and lobby for funding for such research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cone explicitly: (1) support more research on peer-review, (2) urge societies to lobby for federal support, (3) urge societies to support such research themselves. Empirical work is needed to guide interventions and policy.
